about.title: Chino Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A fall rarely feels like a legal matter in the moment. You are on the floor of a grocery aisle off Central Avenue, or on a cracked walkway outside an apartment near Riverside Drive, and the first thought is whether anything is broken. Later comes the harder question: who was supposed to keep that spot safe? In California, a property owner or business in Chino can be held responsible when they knew about a hazard, or reasonably should have known, and did nothing to fix it or warn people. That "notice" piece is where these cases are usually won or lost, so photos of the spill, the lighting, the missing handrail, and any warning signs matter enormously. Store video can be overwritten within days unless someone asks for it in writing. We handle premises liability claims in Chino on a contingency basis, meaning there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I tripped on a broken sidewalk in Chino. Is the city responsible?
items.answer: It depends on who owns and maintains that stretch of sidewalk, which in Chino could be the city, San Bernardino County, or an adjacent private property owner. Claims against a public entity in California generally must be filed within six months, far sooner than the two-year deadline for private owners. Photograph the exact spot and its surroundings so the location can be pinned down quickly. We can help identify the right party before that short window closes.

items.question: The store says I should have watched where I was walking. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: No. California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you are found partly responsible, you can still recover, reduced by your share of the blame. The store still has to answer for whether it knew about the hazard and failed to fix or warn. A partial fault argument is common and does not mean the case is over.

items.question: What should I do in the first few days after a fall?
items.answer: Get medical care and describe the fall accurately so it is in your records. Photograph the hazard, the lighting, and any signage, and get names of anyone who saw what happened. Ask the business for an incident report and request in writing that they save all camera footage. Then reach out, and we can take it from there.
